Usually derived from Old Lithuanian elenis (“deer”,modern from Lithuanian élnias),from Proto-Indo-European ⋆h₁el-. This derivation is supported by the fact that the from Middle High German el(e)n form appears during a time when the elk was gradually dying out in the German-speaking lands. Das '''Elter''' ist oft erschöpft.:translationThe children recognize the sound of speech,the tone of voice,and know how high the noise level will be when they close the front door behind them carrying their bags and other essentials. The '''parent''' is often exhausted.:titleFamilie - ein Symbol der Kultur:page182:authorSusanne Weinert Portmann|Usage notes}''Elter'' is not widely used outside the field of genetics; in other contexts,''Elternteil'' is more common. *Eltern*de{}|Alternative forms}Aeltern|Etymology}From Middle High German eltern,from Old High German eltirōn,from Proto-Germanic ⋆alþizô. Compare from Dutch ouders,from English elders.}The form is equivalent to a nominalised comparative of alt. The according spelling  was common in Early Modern German,but later went out of fashion. Several sources claim that this was due to incomprehension of the etymology,but that seems implausible given its obviousness. An alternative explanation would be the desire to distinguish between  and ,which latter was commonly spelt .|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈʔɛl.tɐn}De-Eltern.ogg(Germany)}De-at-Eltern.ogg(Austria)|Noun}p)}#parents|Usage notes}#When a singular is required,the term Elternteil is used in everyday language. *emp-*de{}|Etymology}Assimilation of ent- before ''f-''. In Middle High German,assimilated and non-assimilated forms were used interchangeably; compare from Middle High German enphinden alongside from Middle High German entvinden. Eventually,the form ''emp-'' became standardised in three verb stems. Compare the similar assimilation ''-ntb-'' → ''-mp-'' in empor,Wimper,and Himper (archaic variant of Himbeere).|Pronunciation}IPA:/ɛmp/|Prefix}emp-:}#ent-'',only used in empfangen,empfehlen,empfinden,and derivatives of these.''|Derived terms}prefixsee:de

*-end*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German -ende,from Old High German -enti,from Old High German -anti,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆-andī,from Proto-Germanic pospresent participle ending. Cognate with from Dutch -end,from Old English -ende. See from English -and,from English -ing for more.}The gerundive use of the present participle goes back to the dative form of the Middle High German infinitive,which was sometimes enhanced with ''-d-'' through interaction with the present participle:from Middle High German tto read. Placed before the noun,this construction was then reinterpreted as actually involving a participle,which lead to grammatical agreement:from Middle High German das zu lesende Buch,and thus by analogy from Middle High German ta book to be read. Compare the etymologically correct construction in from Dutch het/een te lezen boek.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ənt/}Ⓓd/d0/LL-Q188_%28deu%29-Frank_C._M%C3%BCller--end.wav|Suffix}-end:}#A suffix forming the present participle of German verbs,analogous to cog+en+-ing.}•Wein'''end''' rief sie bei mir an.}•Crying,she called me on the telephone.}•Die tanz'''end'''en Mädchen sind hübsch.}•The dancing girls are pretty.}•Er inseriert die zu vermiet'''end'''e Wohnung.}•He places an advert for the flat to be let out.}•qGerundive use,cf. etymology above

*Engerling*de{}slim-wikipedia:langde}ine-pro|Alternative forms}Emmerling qual:dated or regional|Etymology}From Middle High German engerlinc,from Old High German engiring (10th c.),diminutive of from Old High German angar ‘large larva’ (compare modern dialectal Anger,Inger),from Proto-Germanic ⋆angaraz,from Proto-Indo-European ⋆h₂engʷʰ-ir- (compare from Lithuanian ungurỹs ‘eel’,from Lithuanian ánkštara,from Lithuanian inkstìras ‘pimple; tapeworm’,Albanian from Albanian thnegël ‘ant’). Compare also Unke,ultimately from a variant of the same Indo-European root.|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈʔɛŋɐlɪŋ}Ⓓe/e3/De-Engerling.ogg|Noun}(mask.)}#ng:superfamily,for example the European cockchafers,the summer chafers,the garden chafer or the European rhinoceros beetle.}#dated ng:family,including the botflies,warbleflies and gadflies.}#}Engerling :de:firstSigmund :lastSchenkling :title Die Bekämpfung der Dasselplage:journalDeutsche entomologische National-Bibliothek :Rundschau im Gebiete der Insektenkunde mit besonderer Berücksichtigung der Literatur:locationBerlin-Dahlem :year1911 :volume2:issue17:pages134-135 :urlhttps://sdei.senckenberg.de/media/openaccess/01278.pdf:passage  Hier finden sich dann die Dasselbeulen,etwa sechs Monate nach dem Schwärmen der Fliegen,also im Januar bis zum Frühjahr. Die Beulen erreichen die Größe einer Walnuß und weisen bei der Reife seitlich eine kleine Öffnung auf,aus der eine klebrige Flüssigkeit hervortritt. In diesen Beulen sitzen die Larven,von den Landleuten „'''Engerlinge'''“ genannt.:translationHere the warbles appear,approximately six months after the swarming of the adult,thus in January until the Spring. The swellings reach the size of a walnut and upon maturity exhibit a small opening at the side,from which a sticky fluid emerges. In these swellings reside the larvae,known to the country folk as "'''grubs'''".

*-ens*de{}|Suffix}-ens:}#plural suffix for family names that end in a sibilant consonant}•''Schmitz'' → ''(die) Schmitz'''ens''''' (“the Schmitz'''es''',“the Schmitz family”)}•''Pütz'' → ''(die) Pütz'''ens''''' (“the Pütz'''es''',“the Pütz family”)|Suffix}-ens:}#dated genitive suffix for personal names that end in a sibilant consonant}•''Max'' → ''Max'''ens''' Vater'' (“Max'''’s''' father”)}•''Klaus'' → ''Klaus'''ens''' Mutter'' (“Klaus'''’s''' mother”)}#dated genitive suffix for personal names that end in ''-ia''}•''Claudia'' → ''Claudi'''ens''' Tochter'' (“Claudia'''’s''' daughter”)}•''Maria'' → ''Mari'''ens''' Sohn'' (“Mary'''’s''' son”)|Usage notes}In contemporary usage the genitive is usually left unchanged after sibilants,and indicated with an apostrophe in writing:''Max’ Vater''. Such unchanged genitives,in turn,are often avoided and paraphrased:''der Vater von Max'' (colloquially:''vom Max'').}The genitive is formed with -s after ''-ia'':''Claudias,Marias''. Only the form Mariens remains current,but it is restricted to the Virgin Mary.|Suffix}-ens:}#forms adverbs from superlatives and ordinal numbers}•''der'' erste → erstens}•''am'' meisten → meistens}•''am'' besten → bestens}•''am'' frühesten → frühestens|Usage notes}Adverbs in ''-ens'' often have an absolute superlative sense,meaning “at most,maximally” or “very much,exceedingly”. These forms are widely lexicalized,however. That is to say that they cannot be formed freely,except in poetic or humorous language.

Equivalent to ent+setzen,literally “to put out (of a state,condition)”,whence the two senses of ''to horrify'' (i.e. put out of tranquility) and ''to relieve'' (i.e. put out of a siege). *Erbfeind*de{}2017|Etymology}From Middle High German tthe Devil as the hereditary enemy of mankind. Equivalent to [[[Erbe]+[t1inheritance,heritage]]+[Feind]]+[t2enemy].}Since the 15th century used of the Turks (seen as infidel and followers of the Devil). Then generalised to any long-standing enmity without religious context. The new narrowing to the French is an influence of 19th-century nationalism,which resented France for the Napeolonic invasions and for its general opposition to German national unity. This narrowing was never absolute,however,and the word continued to be used in other contexts.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈɛrpˌfaɪ̯nt/}Ⓓ1/1f/De-Erbfeind.ogg|Noun}(mask.,plural:[Erbfeind(e)s])}#A historical enemy,hereditary (inherited) or sworn enemy believed to be hostile for generations male or of unspecified gender}#}Jakob Kubli,"Marke zeigt vereinigtes Korea",''Neue Zürcher Zeitung'',1 February 2016.}#}:Im Disput zwischen Südkorea und Japan hat sich Nordkorea mit seinem '''Erbfeind''' Südkorea stets solidarisch erklärt.+In the dispute between South Korea and Japan,North Korea declared solidarity with its '''historical enemy''' South Korea every time.}#dated the Devil}•synononym [[[Teufel],[Satan]],[Luzifer]],[Höllenfürst]|Usage notes}In German historic consciousness the term is mostly associated with the French,and by extension the Romans,as supposed hereditary enemies of the Germans/Germanics. This notion was in vogue during the 19th century and the first half of the 20th century.|Derived terms}erbfeindlich}Erbfeindin}Erbfeindlichkeit}Erbfeindschaft

*-erei*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German -erīe,from Old French -erie. The suffix first became productive in German to designate workshops pertaining to occupation names ending in -er,such as Bäckerei from Bäcker. These cases are more properly analyzed as derivations in -ei from the occupation name. Later on,began to be freely attached to verb stems,autonomously from agent nouns. Compare e.g.  above with Backerei derived directly from backen. Similar developments took place in from Dutch -erij and,to a lesser degree,from English -ery.|Pronunciation}IPA:/əˈʁaɪ̯/}Ⓓ7/7b/LL-Q188_%28deu%29-Frank_C._M%C3%BCller--erei.wav|Suffix}-erei:}#Used to form verbal nouns,which often have an informal,frequentative and/or negative overtone.}•synononym ge-}•warten}•singen|Usage notes}This suffix is of virtually unlimited productivity in colloquial German.}Verbs whose stems end in ''-er'' or ''-el'' use the simple suffix -ei instead:

*erst*de{}|Etymology}See the numeral erster.|Pronunciation}IPA:ʔɛɐ̯st}De-at-erst.ogg(Austria)}Ⓓ9/93/De-erst.ogg|Adverb}#first,at first}•synononym zuerst}#only with progress,accomplishments or the present time}•Sie ist '''erst''' 28 Jahre alt.}•She is '''only''' 28 years old.}•Es ist '''erst''' halb zehn.}•It is '''only''' half past nine.}#not until,not for,not before with reference to a point or period of time in the future}•Ich bin '''erst''' nächsten Monat in Urlaub.}•I'm '''not''' on vacation '''until''' next month.}•Mein Bruder kommt '''erst''' in drei Wochen an.}•My brother's '''not''' arriving '''for''' three weeks.}#only,as recently as with reference to the past}•Er ist '''erst''' gestern gegangen.}•He left '''only''' yesterday.}•Er ist '''erst''' seit zwei Tagen da.}•He has '''only''' been here for two days.}#short for [erstmal]}•Es ist kalt im Süden. Und im Norden '''erst'''!}•It is cold in the South. And '''especially''' in the North.}#Switzerland zumal}#}erst Wer lieber Arthousefilme streamt,findet bei Filmingo,Myfilm und  Cinefile lokale Alternativen,die '''erst''' noch regelmässig ihre Steuern zahlen.|Usage notes}With reference to time periods and moments,the opposite of erst is schon. ''Erst'' emphasizes how ''long'' it is until something happens or how ''recently'' it has happened,whereas schon how ''soon'' in the future or ''far'' in the past. Thus:}:'''erst''' in drei Wochen}•not for three weeks}:'''schon''' in drei Wochen}•in only three weeks}With reference to progress and the like,erst emphasizes how young or short,while schon emphasizes how old or long. Thus:}:Sie ist '''erst''' 28 Jahre alt}•She's only 28}:Sie ist '''schon''' 28 Jahre alt}•She's already 28|Derived terms}erst recht

*Erweis*de{}|Etymology}From erweisen.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ɛɐ̯ˈvaɪ̯s/}Er+weis}Ⓓ3/3d/De-Erweis.ogg|Noun}(mask.)}#dated proof
*-erweise*de{}|Alternative forms}-er Weise|Etymology}From the genitive feminine singular adjective ending  and the feminine noun Weise. This was originally an adverbial genitive first used in Middle High German. For example,nointerptrue. Adverbs formed this way represent univerbations of genitive absolute adjective-noun phrases.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ɐˌvaɪ̯zə/|Suffix}-erweise:}#Used to form adverbs from adjectives and participles; these adverbs are used to modify phrases or sentences. Cognate with English -wise.}•normal}•traurig}•lustig}•gleich|Usage notes}A normal German adverb,which modifies verbs,nouns,adjectives,or (other) adverbs,is identical to the basic form of the respective adjective. Only when an adverb refers to a whole phrase or sentence does it take the ending ''-erweise''. The distinction may be semantic. Compare:}: (He felt sad as he returned to his homeland.)}: (It is sad that he returned to his homeland.)|Derived terms}suffixsee:de|See also}-weise

*etwa*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German etwā,contraction of from Middle High German etewā (also from Middle High German eteswā),from tsomewhere. For the first component compare etlich,etwas; the second is wo. A related formation was from Middle High German ete(s)wanne,in which the second component is wann. The Middle Dutch spellings indeed seem to point to a back vowel; on the other hand there is no certainty about this and the modern front-rounded vowel would remain unexplained. An alternative theory derives it from Proto-West Germanic tup,at the top+from Proto-West Germanic ⋆-īn. This explains the umlaut,but is still at odds with the dialectal pronunciation ˈøˑʏ̯pə ~ ˈøːpə,which would require West-Germanic from Proto-West Germanic au-. *-euse*de{}|Etymology}Borrowed fr.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈøːzə/}Ⓓ2/27/De--euse.ogg|Suffix}-euse:}#-eur.}•synononym -eurin|Usage notes}Feminine forms in m:-euse can be formed freely,but their stylistic values differ:Certain forms could only be considered humorous (e.g.  from Monteur). In some other cases the form in  is considered more respectful and professional; for example,Friseurin,Masseurin are now preferred over Friseuse,Masseuse,which may have a vaguely dismissive tone. Yet other forms like Souffleuse do not show this tendency and are entirely usual.

*eventualiter*de{}|Etymology}Borrowed NL.. So used because Cognate German eventuell is now used to mean etwaig,allfällig.|Pronunciation}Ⓓb/ba/De-eventualiter.ogg|Adverb}#literary eventually,in the end}•synononym [[[[letztlich],[am Ende]],[schließlich]],[schlussendlich]],[letztendlich]}#}eventualiter :de:date26-06-2020:workw:langde:Archiv für die civilistische Praxis (AcP)|volume220|issue2|authorJürgen Kohler|titleSchadensersatz durch Vindikationspreisgabe nach § 281 Abs. 4 BGB|doi10.1628/acp-2020-0008|pages151–152|passageHätte der Gesetzgeber die Wirkungsweise des § 283 Abs. 1 BGB a.F. richtig gewürdigt,wäre bemerkt worden,dass die Regelung nicht nur wesentlich von dem in § 281 Abs. 4 BGB vorgesehenen Konzept abweicht,sondern prozessuale Umständlichkeit und damit auch Langwierigkeit,aber auch Kostspieligkeit regelmäßig gerade vermeidet. Denn bei bestrittener,aber vom Beklagten '''eventualiter''' zu vertretender Erfüllungsunmöglichkeit konnte der Beklagte dank des § 283 Abs. 1 BGB a.F. zum Einen ohne Ermittlung der Erfüllungsmöglichkeit zur Erfüllungsleistung verurteilt werden. Zum Anderen blieb dem Kläger bei bestrittener Leistungsmöglichkeit erspart,seinen Prozesserfolg nur durch die Opferung des Erfüllungsanspruchs zu sichern,indem er seinerseits ebenfalls Leistungsunmöglichkeit behauptet und er sich daher mit Schadensersatz begnügt.

*extra*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈɛks.tʁa/}De-at-extra.ogg(Austria)}Ⓓc/c9/De-extra.ogg|Adjective}#colloquial extra-}•Das is’n ganz '''extra''' Rezept von meiner Mutter.}•This is a very '''special''' recipe of my mother’s.|Usage notes}In formal standard German,''extra-'' is a prefix attached to the following noun. In colloquial German,however,it is often treated like a real adjective. Der Tee is’ '''extra''' heiß!}•Be careful! The tea is extra hot!|Usage notes}In the sense of “specifically”,''extra'' has entered the standard language and is now frequently seen in writing. The other senses remain colloquial.

*fahl*de{}|Alternative forms}falb|Etymology}From Middle High German val (inflected from Middle High German valwe),from Old High German falo,from Proto-Germanic ⋆falwaz. While the variant falb is from the Middle High German inflected stem,the form  is based on the uninflected stem. However,the lengthened vowel points to influence by varieties that reduce ''-lw-'' to ''-l-'' even in open syllables; these include from Middle Low German vāl (declined from Middle Low German vāle),from Old Saxon falu. See the same development in kahl. *fahren*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German varn,from Middle High German varen,from Old High German faran,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆faran. Cognate with from Dutch varen,from English fare,from Danish fare.|Pronunciation}IPA:aastandard}IPA:aacolloquial,particularly northern and central Germany}De-fahren.ogg(Germany)}De-fahren2.ogg(Germany)}De-at-fahren.ogg(Austria)}aːʁən|Verb}fahren(fährt#fuhr,gefahren,führe,auxiliary:haben,sein)}#chiefly to go at speed}•Der Fuchs '''fährt''' aus dem Bau.}•The fox '''dashes''' from his kennel.}•aus der Haut '''fahren'''}•to fly off the handle}•'''fly''' off the handle}•einen '''fahren''' lassen}•to blow off,to break wind}•Die Sonne '''fährt''' über das Himmelszelt.}•The sun '''moves''' athwart the firmament.}#intransitive to go; to run; to drive; to sail}•Autos können schneller '''fahren''' als Fahrräder.}•Cars can '''go''' faster than bikes.}#intransitive to leave; to depart}#:Beeil dich! Der Zug '''fährt''' jetzt gleich.}•Hurry up! The train is '''departing''' in a moment.}#:synononym abfahren}#intransitive to go by vehicle; to sail; to travel}•Er '''fährt''' wie ein Bekloppter.}•He '''drives''' like a maniac.}•Wir '''fahren''' diesen Sommer nach Holland.}• We'''’re going''' to Holland this summer. Implying a trip by car,bike,train,or ship.}#intransitive to leave and therefor use a vehicle}#:Wir '''fahren''' jetzt.}•We'''’re leaving''' now. (Implying the use of a vehicle.)}#transitive to drive; to ride; to sail (a vehicle)}#:Sie '''fährt''' einen roten Wagen.}•She '''drives''' a red car.}#transitive to take (someone somewhere by vehicle); to drive; to transport}#:Ich '''fahre''' dich zum Bahnhof.}•I’ll '''take''' you to the train station.}#:synononym führen|Usage notes}In intransitive uses,the perfect auxiliary is always sein:''Wir '''sind''' diesen Sommer nach Holland gefahren.''}In transitive uses,the perfect auxiliary ought to be haben according to standard grammar:''Sie '''hat''' einen roten Wagen gefahren.'' However,''sein'' is also used,chiefly in (colloquial) speech:''Sie '''ist''' einen roten Wagen gefahren.''|Derived terms}col-auto:Fahrgeschäft|See also}gehen

*falls*de{}|Etymology}Presumably from the genitive of Fall.|Pronunciation}IPA:/fals/}Ⓓb/bf/De-falls.ogg|Conjunction}falls:}#conditional if,in the event that}•'''Falls''' es anfängt zu regnen,müssen wir das Fenster zumachen.}•'''If''' it starts raining,we need to close the window.}•'''Falls''' es keinen Nebel gibt,genießen Sie die Sonne.}•'''If''' there is no fog,enjoy the sun.}#chiefly in case,in order to be; prepared if}•Lass uns das Fenster zumachen,'''falls''' es anfängt zu regnen.}•Let's close the window,'''in case''' it starts raining.|Usage notes}''Falls'' is synonymous to the more common wenn,but has the advantage of being unambiguously conditional,while ''wenn'' can also be used temporally (meaning "when,whenever").}Colloquially,''falls'' is used somewhat differently than in standard German proper. It does occur in sense 1,but infrequently. In return,it is often heard in sense 2 where formal usage would require für den Fall,dass.|Synonyms}qualifier:sense 1 wenn}qualifier:sense 2 für den Fall,dass
*-falls*de{}|Etymology}Suffixation of the conjunction falls,this presumably from the genitive of Fall.|Pronunciation}IPA:/fals/|Suffix}-falls:}#ng:used to form adverbs from adjectives<ref name"Leo Grammatik"> https://dict.leo.org/grammatik/deutsch/Wortbildungsregeln/Derivation/To-Adv/Suffixe/falls.xml?langen#id2.1.4.6.3</ref>}•gleich}•besten}•notwendig}#ng:used to form adverbs from pronouns<ref name"Leo Grammatik"></ref>}•kein}•ander|Usage notes}This suffix forms adverbs that imply a particular condition or circumstance,similarly to phrases like "in case of," "if," or "in the event of" in English,and it adds a hypothetical or conditional sense to words.}The adverbs are formed either from an adjective or from a pronoun.}Since the suffix comes from a genitive formation,adjectives are often accompanied by an interfix -en,which originally corresponds to the strong masculine singular declension of the adjective itself.}For the same reason,some pronouns could present the interfix -es,as in keinesfalls.|Derived terms}suffixsee:de

*falten*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German valden,from Middle High German valten,from Old High German faldan,from Old High German faltan,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆falþan. The irregular forms with ''-t-'' arose through early levelling of Grammatischer Wechsel,but remained rare in both Old and Middle High German. They probably established themselves in modern German by analogy as there are several verbs in ''-alten'' (halten,schalten,spalten,walten),but none in ''-alden''.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈfaltən/}De-at-falten.ogg(Austria)}Ⓓe/ed/De-falten.ogg}Rhymes:altn̩|Verb}falten(faltete,gefaltet:gefaltenregional)}#to fold}•seine Hände '''falten'''}•to '''fold''' one's hands}•mit '''gefalteten''' Händen}•with '''folded''' hands|Usage notes}The normal past participle is gefaltet. *fangen*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German vāhen,from Old High German fāhan,a strong verb with past forms from Old High German fieng,from Old High German gefangan,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆fą̄han,from Proto-Germanic ⋆fanhaną. The present stem ''fang-'' is derived from the past forms. This development spread from Middle Low German vangen to Central German dialects of early modern German (compare already from Old Saxon fangan alongside from Old Saxon fāhan). The same happened in hängen (< ''hāhen''),in which,however,the development was reinforced by the existence of two variant verbs and therefore established itself much faster than it did in ''fangen''. (Still today from Alemannic German foo is used in many dialects of Swiss German.) Any information on the sense development?}Antwort:Fechten refers to the sport of fencing,not yard fencing.}Antwort2:The translation notes that it’s cant (of thieves). According to Duden it’s origin is from Rotwelsch (the German thieves' cant) and this explicitly means begging by going from door to door,named after journeymen showing off their fencing skills for money. Duden marks it as colloquialism and dated. *Ferkel*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German verhelīn,from Old High German farhilī,from Old High German farhilīn,diminutive of from Old High German tpig,from Proto-Germanic ⋆farhaz,whence from English farrow.}The ''-k-'' has been explained as an irregular fortition of ''-h-'',which would be plausible if the form were of Upper German origin,where ''-h-'' was strong and where there was dialectal variation between ''-rch-'' and ''-rk-''. However,from Middle High German verkelen is first found in West Central German along the Rhine,where stem-internal ''-h-'' had been lost early on (compare accordingly from Middle High German verlīn). It therefore seems at least equally probable that the ''-k-'' is due to influence by a related Rhenish word for “pig,piglet”,still found today in Ripuarian from Central Franconian Ferke,which goes back to a from German ⋆far(i)kīn (compare from Old Dutch farkīn,from Old Dutch ferkīn,whence modern from Dutch varken),from Proto-Germanic ⋆farhikīną,another diminutive of from Proto-Germanic ⋆farhaz.|Pronunciation}IPA:-kəl}Ⓓ0/0b/De-Ferkel.ogg|Noun}(neut.,diminituve:Ferkel)}#piglet; a young/immature pig}#pejorative A dirty or contemptible person}•synononym [Stinktier],[Sau]|Derived terms}Hirschferkel
